s1.syndrome_frame: Progressive skin lesions with systemic involvement
salient_findings: Purpura and ecchymoses with progression over 12 months
Waxy yellow papules and plaques with purpura in multiple regions
Abnormal liver function test results and renal impairment
key_facts: 1-year history of purpura, ecchymoses, anorexia, and weight loss
Medical history of alcohol abuse and cognitive impairment
Purpura and ecchymoses initially periorbital, then progressed
Elder abuse was excluded
Anemia, abnormal liver function test results, and renal impairment with moderate proteinuria
Normal serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) and immunofixation urine protein electrophoresis test results
Radiological studies were unremarkable
4-mm punch biopsy showed upper dermal amorphous eosinophilic deposits
Congo red staining was positive
Polarizing light microscopy demonstrated pale apple-green birefringence

shortlist.label: Primary systemic amyloidosis
shortlist.why_kept: Positive Congo red staining and polarizing light microscopy demonstrating apple-green birefringence, consistent with amyloid deposits

shortlist.label: Lipoid proteinosis
shortlist.why_kept: Waxy yellow papules and plaques with purpura, consistent with clinical presentation of lipoid proteinosis

shortlist.label: Secondary systemic amyloidosis
shortlist.why_kept: Chronic disease and systemic involvement, potentially leading to secondary amyloidosis

shortlist.label: Amyloidosis associated with multiple myeloma
shortlist.why_kept: Although SPEP and immunofixation were normal, amyloidosis associated with multiple myeloma remains a consideration given the patient's age and systemic symptoms

shortlist.label: Familial amyloid polyneuropathy
shortlist.why_kept: Systemic involvement and amyloid deposits, although less likely given the lack of prominent neuropathic symptoms

raw.rationale: The patient's presentation with purpura, ecchymoses, anorexia, weight loss, and the biopsy findings of upper dermal amorphous eosinophilic deposits with positive Congo red staining and pale apple-green birefringence under polarizing light microscopy are characteristic of amyloidosis. The absence of multiple myeloma (normal SPEP and immunofixation) and the lack of a clear familial component or neuropathy make primary systemic amyloidosis the most likely diagnosis.

rejected.label: Lipoid proteinosis
rejected.why: While lipoid proteinosis can present with skin lesions and can involve other organs, the specific findings of amyloid deposits on biopsy and the systemic nature of the symptoms point more towards an amyloidosis diagnosis.

rejected.label: Secondary systemic amyloidosis
rejected.why: This condition is typically associated with chronic inflammatory diseases or infections, which are not mentioned in the patient's history.

rejected.label: Amyloidosis associated with multiple myeloma
rejected.why: Normal serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) and immunofixation urine protein electrophoresis test results make this diagnosis less likely.

rejected.label: Familial amyloid polyneuropathy
rejected.why: The patient's presentation lacks the characteristic neuropathy, and there's no mention of a familial component or specific mutations associated with this condition.
